title: The Jazz Singer was mostly silent
hook: The film remembered as the first talkie has only about two minutes of talking.
peek: The Jazz Singer of 1927 is often called the first talking picture. Most of it is actually a silent film with title cards and a recorded score. The spoken lines that made history were short, and largely improvised by its star, Al Jolson.
lede: When Warner Bros. released The Jazz Singer in October 1927, it was not planned as a talking picture. It was a silent film with a recorded orchestral score and several songs sung by Al Jolson, all synchronised to the picture. Between the songs, Jolson ad-libbed a little speech. Those few spoken moments, about two minutes in all, changed the film industry.

bullets.text: Jolson's most famous line comes after his first song, when he tells the cheering crowd to wait, because they ain't heard nothin' yet. It was a catchphrase from his stage act, and it suddenly sounded like a promise about cinema itself.

In the longest talking scene, Jolson's character sings to his mother at the piano and chats with her between verses. His father walks in and says a single word, stop, and the film drops back into silence with title cards.

The sound did not sit on the film. It came from large records, each matched to one reel, played on a turntable linked to the projector. If a reel was damaged and trimmed, the voices could fall out of step with the lips.

Warner Bros. had already released Don Juan in 1926 with a recorded score but no dialogue. The first feature with talking all the way through came in 1928: Lights of New York, a short crime drama that was a big hit.
